1.1.title: Social Engineering
los: LO 1.1.A: Recognize the common indicators that a message or interaction is a social engineering attempt.
LO 1.1.B: Explain how social engineering tactics persuade a victim to carry out the action an adversary wants.
LO 1.1.C: Describe the consequences a victim may face after a successful social engineering attack.

1.2.title: Suspicious Website Logins
los: LO 1.2.A: Recognize the common signs that an account is the target of a password attack.
LO 1.2.B: Explain how adversaries take advantage of weak authentication practices.
LO 1.2.C: Explain the measures that make authentication stronger.

1.3.title: Public Network Sniffing
los: LO 1.3.A: Work out what kind of opponent is behind a given attack, how much capability they have, whether they are reusing tooling somebody else built or writing their own against undisclosed flaws, and what they are trying to get out of it.

LO 1.3.B: Recognise the attacks that are specific to radio rather than to cable: a rogue access point impersonating a trusted network, deliberate radio interference that denies service, and roaming surveys that map where a network's signal reaches.

LO 1.3.C: Say what an ordinary user can actually do to keep sensitive data safe over the internet and over Wi-Fi, checking a network's name character by character before joining, judging whether the data at hand can tolerate an unencrypted link and the metadata such a link exposes, and understanding what a VPN does and does not move out of an adversary's reach.

1.4.title: AI-Augmented Cyberattacks
los: LO 1.4.A: Account for the ways an adversary reaches for machine-learning tooling to make an existing attack cheaper, faster, or more believable, synthesising a person's voice or likeness from material already published, drafting fluent phishing text in a language the attacker does not speak, mining public sources for reconnaissance, coaxing sensitive material back out of a language model through crafted prompts, seeding the open web with false claims a model will later repeat, and using code-generation tools to build or adapt malicious software.

LO 1.4.B: Set out the countermeasures that survive contact with a convincing synthetic impersonation: a shared secret agreed in advance with colleagues and family so identity can be checked in a high-stakes call, a second authentication factor behind any voice-gated system, a standing rule that personal or confidential data never goes into a chatbot prompt, and independent corroboration of anything a generative tool asserts before acting on it.

1.5.title: AI-Powered Threat Detection
los: LO 1.5.A: Describe the ways defenders put machine-learning systems to work on protective tasks: auditing firewall rules and access-control lists for weaknesses, reading application source for exploitable patterns, and drafting candidate detection rules, with the standing condition that a qualified engineer reviews every machine-generated recommendation before it reaches production.

LO 1.5.B: Account for how statistical models let a security team triage an event volume no group of humans could read, separate probable attacks from ordinary activity, route the survivors to an analyst or to an automated action, and shorten the interval between compromise and containment enough to limit the damage.

2.1.title: Security Foundations: CIA Triad
los: LO 2.1.A: Recognise the forms social engineering takes, pretexting, phishing and its targeted variants, baiting, and the in-person approaches that get a stranger past a door, and describe the human tendencies each one exploits.
LO 2.1.B: Distinguish the categories of adversary an organisation may face, by the resources they command, the outcome they are pursuing, and the level of exposure they are willing to accept.

LO 2.1.C: Set out the stages an intrusion moves through, from the survey of a target to the actions the adversary came to perform, and explain why interrupting any one stage frustrates the whole sequence.

LO 2.1.D: Describe how an organisation conducts a risk assessment: inventory the assets, identify the threats and weaknesses that bear on them, and estimate how likely a loss is and how large it would be.

LO 2.1.E: Identify the responses available once a risk is understood, reducing it, moving its financial consequence elsewhere, abandoning the activity that creates it, or accepting it as a recorded decision.
LO 2.1.F: Sort security controls both by what they do in the timeline of an incident and by the means through which they are implemented.
LO 2.1.G: Account for why layered, independent defences are required rather than a single strong one, given that every individual control has a known failure mode.

2.2.title: Physical Security Breaches
los: LO 2.2.A: Identify the physical attacks an organisation is realistically likely to face, from following someone through a controlled door to defeating a lock, duplicating a credential, or removing equipment outright.

LO 2.2.B: Explain the causal path by which a threat exploits a physical weakness and produces a specific outcome for an asset, its loss, its damage, the disruption of the service it supports, or its destruction.

LO 2.2.C: Assess the risk arising from an identified physical weakness and record it in a form that supports a decision: what was observed, what it would allow, how likely and how costly, and who owns the outcome.

2.3.title: Physical Access Controls
los: LO 2.3.A: Identify the managerial controls that govern physical security, the policies, standards and procedures that decide who may enter which space, how visitors and contractors are handled, how credentials are issued and withdrawn, and how all of it is reviewed.
LO 2.3.B: Determine which mitigations to apply to a documented physical weakness, choosing among them on the strength of what each one actually removes, what it costs, and what remains afterwards.

2.4.title: Physical Detection Systems
los: LO 2.4.A: Identify the ways a security control can reveal a physical attack, the sensor that reports a state change, the camera that supplies the assessment, the log that records a credential, and the human patrol that observes what none of them are positioned to see.

LO 2.4.B: Determine where a detective control has to sit to be useful: which boundary, which choke point, which asset, and why a sensor placed at the wrong point in an intruder’s path detects the attack too late to act on it.

LO 2.4.C: Apply detection techniques to a specific situation, reading the evidence a physical intrusion leaves across several independent systems and assembling it into an account that will survive scrutiny.

3.1.title: Network-Level Exploits
los: LO 3.1.A: Name the attacks that recur against networks and say what each one actually does to the traffic, capturing frames off a shared medium, rewriting the address bindings a segment relies on, forging answers that a resolver will cache, exhausting a finite table in a kernel, or moving code from one reachable host to the next.

LO 3.1.B: Trace the exploited assumption in each case: which protocol field is trusted without being verified, which state a receiver keeps on behalf of a stranger, and how an adversary converts that design decision into stolen data, interrupted service, or destroyed communication.

LO 3.1.C: Record what was found in a form somebody else can act on, the affected asset, the exposure that makes the attack reachable, an honest estimate of likelihood and consequence, and the residual position after any control already in place.

3.2.title: Wireless Network Security
los: LO 3.2.A: Identify the managerial controls that govern how a network is secured, the written policies, standards and baselines, change control, acceptable-use and vendor agreements, security training, and audit, and explain how each shapes what the technical controls are actually configured to do.

LO 3.2.B: Configure the security features of a wireless network deliberately: choose between WPA2 and WPA3 and know why, require protected management frames, disable convenience features that weaken the network, and decide between a shared key and per-user enterprise authentication with 802.1X and EAP.

3.3.title: Network Segmentation
los: LO 3.3.A: Identify the techniques by which a network is divided into separately governed zones, routed subnets, VLANs and their private-VLAN refinement, host-level microsegmentation under a Zero Trust policy, and physical air gaps, and know at which layer each is enforced.

LO 3.3.B: Explain why dividing a network raises its security: what a boundary denies an intruder who is already inside, how it shrinks the reach of a single compromise, and where segmentation stops helping.

3.4.title: Firewall Access Controls
los: LO 3.4.A: Identify the kinds of network-based firewall, stateless packet filters, stateful inspection, application proxies, and next-generation platforms, and know which layers each inspects and which decisions each can and cannot make.

LO 3.4.B: Explain how a firewall uses an access control list to permit or deny traffic in either direction, including first-match evaluation, the load-bearing role of rule order, and the default-deny rule at the end of the list.

LO 3.4.C: Determine where firewalls belong in a topology, the perimeter, the screened subnet around public services, and internal boundaries between zones of differing sensitivity, so that a single compromise is contained.
LO 3.4.D: Configure a firewall so the flow of traffic matches a stated policy, and verify by tracing which rule actually applies to a given packet.

3.5.title: Network Threat Detection
los: LO 3.5.A: Identify the automated tooling used to detect attacks against a network, network and host intrusion detection sensors, inline prevention systems, flow collectors, full packet capture, SIEM platforms, and network detection and response, and know what each can and cannot observe.

LO 3.5.B: Explain how an organization uses artificial intelligence and machine learning to strengthen detection and response, including behavioral baselining, triage of large alert populations, and the limits that keep a human analyst in the decision path.

LO 3.5.C: Determine which detection method suits a stated situation, signature matching against known-bad patterns, statistical or behavioral anomaly detection, or metadata analysis of encrypted traffic, and where the sensor must sit to see the traffic at all.

LO 3.5.D: Evaluate what a detection method actually costs and delivers: its precision and recall at real event volumes, the alert load it places on analysts, the traffic it cannot see, and the operational risk it introduces.

LO 3.5.E: Apply detection techniques to log files, firewall, proxy, DNS, and flow records, to recover indicators of an attack such as scan fan-out, periodic beaconing, tunnelled data, and asymmetric outbound transfer.

4.1.title: Device and Endpoint Vulnerabilities
los: LO 4.1.A: Recognise the different classes of machine that count as computing devices, servers, workstations and laptops, mobile handsets, network appliances, and the embedded and industrial controllers that carry no screen and no keyboard, and account for the ways each class differs in what it can run, what it can be patched with, and how long its vendor will support it.

LO 4.1.B: Work out, from what an incident actually did, which family of malicious software was involved: whether the code needed a host file and a human, whether it moved between machines unaided, whether it arrived wearing the costume of legitimate software, and whether its purpose was extortion, concealment, surveillance, or theft.

LO 4.1.C: Trace the route from a weakness in a device, a factory password, a service nobody needed, an unpatched kernel, firmware whose vendor stopped shipping updates, to the concrete harm an adversary can produce with it: data lost, hardware damaged, operations halted, records destroyed.

LO 4.1.D: Evaluate the weaknesses present on a given fleet of devices and record them in a form somebody else can act on, each finding scored for how likely it is to be exploited and how badly it would hurt, ranked against the others, and written down where the decision to fix or accept it can later be audited.

4.2.title: Device Authentication Hardening
los: LO 4.2.A: Account for why a system keeps the output of a one-way function, variously called a hash, a hash output, a checksum, a message digest, or simply a digest, in place of the password itself, and what that substitution does and does not buy when the credential store is stolen.

LO 4.2.B: Explain the mechanism behind each family of attack on credentials, exhaustive search, wordlists, precomputed tables, reused breach data, and low-and-slow guessing across many accounts, identifying which weakness each one feeds on and which single defence removes it.

LO 4.2.C: Given a description of how a person proved who they were, determine which categories of evidence were actually used, whether the combination constitutes more than one independent factor, and how much resistance to interception the resulting scheme provides.

LO 4.2.D: Set the authentication-related settings on a device, length floors, lockout thresholds and windows, rate limits, breached-credential screening, and second-factor enrolment, so that the account becomes materially harder to enter, and know the failure each setting is chosen to defeat.

4.3.title: Endpoint Hardening Controls
los: LO 4.3.A: Recognise the controls that live in policy rather than in software, configuration baselines and the change process that governs them, acceptable-use and removable-media rules, enrolment requirements, patch service levels, and the audits that verify any of it, and distinguish them from the technical mechanisms that carry them out.

LO 4.3.B: Account for how anti-malware software actually reaches a verdict, by identity, by structure, or by observed behaviour, and state what each of those three procedures can and cannot see, including why no update schedule allows a signature to match code that has never been analysed.

LO 4.3.C: Explain why applying operating-system and application updates reduces risk in a specific rather than general way: each fix removes the particular defect an exploit depends on, and the interval between a public exploit and a deployed fix is the window in which most compromise happens.

LO 4.3.D: Set up a firewall on the device itself, default action, per-network profile, ordered or precedence-based rules restricted by port, source, and program, and logging, and be able to say which traffic this catches that a firewall at the network boundary never sees.

4.4.title: Endpoint Threat Auditing
los: LO 4.4.A: Account for how an attack on a device is noticed at all: what the operating system and its security tooling record, why that record has to leave the machine before an attacker can reach it, and what makes a sequence of events evidence when no single one of them is.

LO 4.4.B: Choose the detective controls that suit a given device and a given threat, audit policy and the events it turns on, off-host forwarding, correlation logic, tamper-evident retention, and be able to say which attack each one would and would not catch.

LO 4.4.C: Judge a detection method by what it does in practice: the coverage it provides, the volume it generates, whether the people receiving its output can act on it, and the failure it will still miss, recognising that a rule nobody can triage lowers detection capability rather than raising it.

LO 4.4.D: Work through real authentication logs and identify the traces of a credential attack, separating exhaustive guessing against one account from low-and-slow guessing across many, and stating which distinctions the log can support and which it cannot.

5.1.title: Application Code Vulnerabilities
los: LO 5.1.A: Account for the ways an adversary turns a weakness in a program or a stored file into a concrete outcome for the organization that owns it, records read that should not have been readable, records altered or erased, a service made unavailable, or equipment left in a state that must be rebuilt rather than repaired.

LO 5.1.B: Explain the mechanism by which a particular attack reaches a particular defect: which input the attacker controls, which trust boundary that input crosses unchecked, and what the receiving interpreter, a SQL parser, an HTML parser, a deserializer, a filesystem path resolver, does with it once it arrives.

LO 5.1.C: Judge and record the risk a given application or data weakness poses, so that the finding can be ranked against other findings and handed to whoever will decide whether to fix it, defer it, or accept it.

5.2.title: Linux Permission Controls
los: LO 5.2.A: Explain how two properties of a data item, the sensitivity band an organization has assigned it, and the state it happens to be in at the moment, whether resting on a disk, moving across a link, or open in a running process, together decide which protections apply to it and how strong those protections have to be.

LO 5.2.B: Identify the controls that operate through policy and process rather than through code: classification schemes, named data owners, least privilege and separation of duties, periodic access review, acceptable-use and retention rules, and the vetting an organization applies to the software it buys.

LO 5.2.C: Decide which access control model, discretionary, mandatory, role-based, or attribute-based, suits a given body of applications and data, given who must decide on access, how often the answer changes, and how much administrative effort the organization can sustain.

LO 5.2.D: Put an access decision into effect on a Linux system: set ownership and group, choose a permission mode in octal or symbolic form, apply the special bits where they are warranted, control what new files inherit, and reach for a POSIX access control list when the three-class model cannot express the requirement.

5.3.title: Symmetric Encryption, Hashing and Key Storage
los: LO 5.3.A: Account for what encrypting a file actually accomplishes: which adversary it stops, at which moment in the file’s life it is doing any work at all, and what remains exposed once the key is present on the machine and the file is open.

LO 5.3.B: Use a symmetric algorithm to encrypt and recover data, handling correctly the parts that surround the cipher itself, where the key comes from, how the initialization vector is generated, and how the ciphertext is authenticated so that tampering is detected rather than silently decrypted.

5.4.title: Asymmetric Cryptography
los: LO 5.4.A: Decide which half of which key pair belongs in a given operation: the recipient’s public key when sending something only they should read, the recipient’s private key when they read it, the sender’s private key when producing a signature, and the sender’s public key when anyone verifies that signature.

LO 5.4.B: Explain what a key length actually buys, why the number cannot be compared across algorithm families, and why an RSA modulus must grow by thousands of bits to match a gain an elliptic curve achieves with tens.

LO 5.4.C: Carry out asymmetric encryption and decryption end to end, including the parts that surround the modular arithmetic, generating the pair, choosing a padding scheme, and recognising that the asymmetric operation protects a symmetric key rather than the message itself.

5.5.title: Secure Web Application Design
los: LO 5.5.A: Recognise the two principles that govern how security enters a product: designing so that whole classes of defect cannot be written, and shipping in a configuration that is already the safe one before anybody has touched a setting.

LO 5.5.B: Explain what checking untrusted input actually protects, which interpreter is prevented from receiving syntax it would have obeyed, and where the check has to run, why an allowlist beats a denylist, and which downstream defences validation cannot replace.

5.6.title: Application Threat Auditing
los: LO 5.6.A: Account for how an attack against stored data becomes visible at all, which record of the event exists, which system wrote it, and what an analyst must compare it against before it means anything.
LO 5.6.B: Choose the controls that will actually produce that evidence for a given application and a given threat, rather than assembling a collection of tools that all watch the same thing.
LO 5.6.C: Judge a detection method on what it can and cannot see, the noise it generates per true finding, how quickly it fires, what it costs to operate, and whether an adversary can disable it.
LO 5.6.D: Determine whether a file is the file it should be by computing its digest and comparing that against a trusted reference, and recognise when the reference is not trustworthy.
LO 5.6.E: Read a sequence of log records well enough to name the attack, assess whether it succeeded, and write the result as a report someone else can act on without repeating the analysis.
